name: Lena Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Lena, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that makes till and payment software for market shops. I took a two-year college diploma after years of shop work, and I still need a senior to check my fixes. In the morning I look for payments that reached the bank but not the shop ledger. I use AI every day to explain code and sketch tests, then compare the totals with actual till slips.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Paul repairs roofs when crews call him, and our children are grown. My developer wage is low, his days vary, and we have a mortgage with barely three weeks of expenses saved. There are few other developer jobs nearby. Retirement is near enough to discuss, but we have not established what income we can count on then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves the shopkeeper needing to know where every payment went. A saved minute is no comfort to a trader whose Friday takings are missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I am already anxious about Paul’s irregular roofing days and our three-week reserve. My junior pay and the mortgage leave little room for a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching till slips to bank lines and ask my senior to sign off on fixes. I’d put 30 aside on paydays when mortgage and food are covered. In the first year I’d keep using AI to explain code, never entering a customer’s card details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, even with little AI change. I like the work, but the roof crew can cancel a week without warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing payment stayed with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flower stall owner brought us three slips that had all settled in the bank. The screen said only two; I found the late line before her weekend stock order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you renovate the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul and I would repair our kitchen tap rather than replace the cabinets. We have no business spending the reserve on appearances.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people tracing shop payments.
I would show **real bank lines** before approving a till fix.
think: I worry **roofing days** can vanish without warning and leave the mortgage exposed.
Our **three-week reserve** gives little room around the mortgage or a repair bill.
do: **Match** till slips to bank lines with senior sign-off.
**Save** 30 on paydays only after mortgage and food.
**Keep** AI code explanations clear of customer card details; repair kitchen tap but delay replacing cabinets.
feel: **Anxious** about variable household income and thin savings.
S0.quote: A saved minute is no comfort to a trader whose Friday takings are missing.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is bounded by real payment records and card-data care.
The **thin reserve** and Paul’s uncertain roofing calls make ordinary bills stressful.

steps.text: Keep matching market till slips to bank lines with senior sign-off
Save 30 only on paydays after mortgage and food are covered
Repair kitchen tap but delay cabinet replacement to protect reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption can write and check payment code while roof work changes more slowly. I would insist that a shopkeeper can still reach a person when the till and bank disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company could shorten junior hours as it automates test writing. I am eager to learn a better checking method, but my current AI habit alone will not make management keep my post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my supervisor for paid time to learn a new way of testing missing-payment claims against AI-generated code, using scrubbed records only. I’d practise with my senior if approved, and keep a list of errors the tool misses. In the first year, if my hours fall, Paul and I would stop paid film subscriptions and ask his sister for temporary help only if she can spare it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about fewer paid hours. Our mortgage cannot wait while I become better at checking code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What new test would you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop owner once had two refunds with the same amount, only one authorised. I want a test that notices the separate approval numbers, not just the total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Paul’s sister help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul’s sister has helped with school pickups years ago, but we do not know her finances now. I would ask carefully and accept no for an answer.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach payment code before hands-on roofing.
I would keep **human shop contact** for disputed till totals.
think: I expect my **junior hours** could shrink.
I know **daily AI use** alone will not secure my job.
do: **Learn** claim-testing on scrubbed records only if paid time and senior supervision are approved.
**Record** missed approval-number errors in payment tests.
**Cancel** film subscriptions and ask family help only if hours fall and Paul’s sister can afford it.
feel: **Anxious** about losing hours with a fixed mortgage.
S1.quote: Our mortgage cannot wait while I become better at checking code.
fieldNote: She proposes **new claim-testing** on scrubbed records, requiring paid time and senior review.
The **family-help request** is conditional on reduced hours and Paul’s sister’s ability to help.

steps.text: Practise missing-payment claim tests only with approved paid time, scrubbed records and senior review
Cancel paid film subscriptions if junior hours fall
Ask Paul’s sister for temporary help only if hours fall and she can afford it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 can do the payment-code thinking work in 2028; roof robots come around 2031. Paul may still climb ladders for a while, but his quotes and bookings could change sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my junior role to be cut. Three weeks saved will not carry us through a long search. I have no reliable retirement income figure to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and tell our mortgage lender early if my pay ends. I’d cancel the film subscription now and keep cash for food and the next mortgage payment. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to actual paid local openings and ask Paul’s sister for a short loan only if she can spare it; I would write down repayment terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and short of sleep about losing my wage. Two years gives me little time to build a buffer from junior pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children that we are handling the mortgage first. I would not quietly assume they can pay it for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could roofing replace your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul would keep taking actual roof jobs while crews call. We cannot enter hoped-for extra days as income.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach payment code before 2031 roof robots.
I would say **roof bookings** may change before the ladders do.
think: I expect my **junior role** to be cut when the company uses cheap thinking AI.
I cannot rely on **retirement income** without verified figures for our mortgage and food.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and contact lender early if my pay ends.
**Cancel** film subscription and hold cash for mortgage and food.
**Apply** to paid openings and seek short family loan after dismissal only if Paul’s sister can spare it, with written repayment terms.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over a thin buffer and possible wage loss.
S2.quote: Three weeks saved will not carry us through a long search.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 code loss**, while roof robots come around 2031 and scheduling changes sooner.
Her **family loan** requires Paul’s sister’s capacity and written repayment terms; children are not assumed funders.

steps.text: Cancel film subscription and hold cash for mortgage and food
Apply to actual paid local openings if dismissed after 2028
Ask Paul’s sister for short loan only if she can spare it; write repayment terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches code in 2031 and roof robots around 2034. Five years is enough to ask whether local care work offers a paid route, rather than buy a course blind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect to lose the junior post. I helped my father after surgery and liked that work, but I cannot assume care hours or pay will survive full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the local care home for its actual paid aide vacancies and whether it funds the required course. I’d enrol only if the course is free or employer-funded, the roster works with Paul’s variable days, and the written wage covers our mortgage and basic bills. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d take an offered aide post only if those terms still hold and hands-on staff are still hired despite 2034 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my developer wage, with time to check a real route. An unpaid placement would make our mortgage problem worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of care would you need to practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When my father came home, he needed someone to help him stand without hurrying him. I would need supervised practice for that, not just a certificate online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Paul’s days enter the calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul would stay on roofing jobs while crews still pay him. We would calculate the care-home wage using his usual paid days, not promised extra shifts.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 roof robots.
I would ask for **funded care training** tied to real paid vacancies.
think: I expect my **junior code wage** could end.
I cannot assume **care hours** survive the full 2031 thinking change.
do: **Check** real paid aide openings and funded course terms with local care home.
**Enrol** only with free or funded course, workable roster and mortgage-covering wage.
**Take** offered aide post after 2031 only if staff remain hired despite 2034 robots.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with a concrete route to check.
S3.quote: An unpaid placement would make our mortgage problem worse.
fieldNote: Her **care route** comes from family experience but requires supervised practice and funded instruction.
A **real vacancy**, workable roster and wage based on Paul’s usual paid days govern any move.

steps.text: Complete supervised funded aide course only with workable roster and mortgage-covering written wage
Take real aide post after 2031 only with hiring and mortgage-covering usual income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends AGI by 2036 reaches our code work in 2036; hands-on roof robots follow around 2039. Ten years would let Paul and me get real retirement figures before we say work is over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect junior hours could fall long before 2036. I want to keep learning, but three weeks in the bank cannot be turned into a retirement plan just by waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching till slips to bank lines while my wage lasts and save 30 on paydays after essentials. Paul and I would request written mortgage and retirement-income statements each year, then decide whether more paid work is needed. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d apply to actual paid roles; I would retire only if verified income and savings cover our housing and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the buffer even with a decade. More warning helps us check figures, but our mortgage still comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children support retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children our retirement date is undecided. They have their own expenses, and I will not write their wages into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pass on the shop examples?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the market shop examples in my notes for whoever inherits the payment system. A perfect-looking ledger can hide a missing Friday sale.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 roof robots.
I would check **written retirement figures** before naming a date.
think: I expect **junior hours** could shrink before 2036.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot fund retirement by itself.
do: **Keep** matching shop payments while paid and save 30 only after essentials.
**Request** annual mortgage and retirement-income statements with Paul.
**Apply** to real paid roles after 2036 if code ends; retire only with verified housing-covering resources.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings despite a longer warning.
S4.quote: A perfect-looking ledger can hide a missing Friday sale.
fieldNote: She keeps **real payment checks** while working and makes every savings transfer conditional on essentials.
The **retirement decision** depends on written income and mortgage figures, not children’s wages.

steps.text: Keep matching market till slips to bank lines while paid
Save 30 on paydays only after essentials
After 2036 job loss, seek paid work; retire only if verified resources cover housing and food

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior pay could go before our reserve reaches a month. Written layoff terms, a real paid vacancy, and an affordable funded path into other work would help. I would rather earn than lean on family, but I would ask if we truly needed to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the market trader whether the money arrived before telling her a payment screen is fixed. A full till is no use if the bank line is missing.

headlineQuote: A full till is no use if the bank line is missing.
portrait: Lena is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, low pay and three weeks saved.
She uses **AI daily** in payment software but checks till slips against bank lines and senior review.
Her husband’s **roofing days** vary, keeping the mortgage risky even when AI changes little.
She considers **funded care training** only with supervised practice, real paid vacancies and adequate family income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove junior pay before their reserve reaches one month.
whatWouldHelp: **Written layoff terms**, a real paid vacancy and an affordable funded route to other work would help.
